name: Temporal Hierarchy of Architectural Prediction Error — How PE Events at Different Timescales Integrate into Architectural Experience
short_description: Seven timescales of architectural PE (milliseconds to centuries); architectural experience constituted by multi-timescale PE superposition; meta-template organizing other templates by temporal scale
structural_pattern: Architectural experience generates prediction errors across a hierarchy of timescales spanning seven orders of magnitude. THE SEVEN TIMESCALES: T-1 MILLISECONDS (50-500ms) — perceptual PE: contour detection (VF1), luminance contrast (L1), rapid material evaluation (T9), acoustic onset (AX1). T-2 SECONDS (1-30s) — motor and navigational PE: motor prediction during movement (TP1), postural adjustment, spatial transitions (TP2, SC3), isovist update (SC2). T-3 MINUTES (1-30 min) — promenade and sequence PE: architectural promenade (SC3), emotional trajectory, navigational PE at choice points (SC1), awe (AX3). T-4 HOURS (1-12 hrs) — occupancy and adaptation PE: dynamic light (L5), thermal drift (MAT2), attention fatigue (T25), social encounters (SC4). T-5 DAYS TO WEEKS — circadian and habituation PE: circadian architecture (L2), seasonal thermal (MAT2), cognitive map formation (T3, SC1). T-6 MONTHS TO YEARS — seasonal and functional PE: seasonal cycles, spatial adaptation, cognitive map maturation. T-7 DECADES TO CENTURIES — aging and cultural PE: material aging (TP3), shearing-layer adaptation, cultural layering. INTEGRATION: The occupant at any moment experiences a SUPERPOSITION of PE signals from multiple timescales simultaneously.
higher_order_principle: Architectural experience is constituted by the integration of prediction error events across seven orders of temporal magnitude. Each timescale has its own PE mechanisms, its own templates, and its own design parameters. The quality of an architectural experience depends on how well PE is managed at EACH timescale AND on how coherently the timescales interact. A building can succeed at one timescale and fail at another. The complete assessment of architectural quality requires evaluation across all seven timescales.

T-1_milliseconds.name: Perceptual PE
T-1_milliseconds.characteristic: Preconscious, automatic, operating on every visual fixation and auditory sample

T-2_seconds.name: Motor and Navigational PE
T-2_seconds.characteristic: Active movement through architecture — each step, turn, threshold crossing

T-4_hours.name: Occupancy and Adaptation PE
T-4_hours.characteristic: Workday, museum visit, day at home — initial PE habituates, building becomes background

T-5_days_to_weeks.name: Circadian and Habituation PE
T-5_days_to_weeks.characteristic: Building shifts from novel to familiar, foreground to background

T-6_months_to_years.name: Seasonal and Functional PE
T-6_months_to_years.characteristic: Temporal depth revealed through seasonal material changes

multi_timescale_superposition: Standing in a medieval cathedral: T-1 delivers contour PE from pointed arches; T-2 delivers postural PE from tilted floor; T-3 delivers promenade PE from sequence just traversed; T-4 delivers current light state; T-5 delivers circadian signal from time of day; T-6 delivers seasonal light quality; T-7 delivers patina of eight centuries. The architectural experience IS this multi-timescale integration.

causal_links.evidence_base: Wittmann (2009, 2016) establishes that subjective time depends on event-encoding density. High PE density at short timescales produces expanded subjective duration. Eagleman (2008) demonstrates time dilation during high-arousal events. The architectural extension — buildings with more PE events per unit time FEEL larger and longer — is theoretically coherent but lacks direct experimental test.

The claim that coherence across timescales produces integrated experience is a theoretical extension by analogy from music cognition. Architectural evidence is phenomenological (Zumthor's 'atmosphere,' Pallasmaa's 'multi-sensory experience') rather than experimental. Most speculative link in TP4.

Buildings can succeed at some timescales and fail at others. A glass tower may produce excellent visual PE (T-1/T-2) but catastrophic circadian disruption (T-5) and negative aging trajectory (T-7). Each timescale failure has its own diagnostic mechanism and template.

scope_conditions: This is a META-template — it organizes existing templates by temporal scale rather than introducing new mechanisms
All seven timescales are always present; the question is which are salient at any given moment
Shorter timescales (T-1 through T-3) dominate during active exploration; longer timescales (T-5 through T-7) dominate during extended occupancy
The hierarchy is approximately logarithmic in time — each level spans roughly one order of magnitude
moderators: Occupancy mode: visitor (T-1 through T-3 dominant) vs. daily occupant (T-4 through T-5 dominant) vs. long-term resident (T-5 through T-7 dominant)
Movement vs. stillness: movement activates T-2 and T-3; stillness suppresses them and elevates T-4/T-5
Attention: focused attention on short timescales reduces awareness of longer timescales and vice versa
Expertise: architectural experts may attend to longer timescales (material aging, spatial adaptation) more readily than naive occupants

interactions.nature: TP1 operates primarily at T-2 (motor PE during movement). TP4 situates it within the broader temporal hierarchy.
TP2 operates at T-2/T-3 (threshold crossing as episodic boundary). TP4 shows that thresholds are the temporal joints that segment T-3 level experience.
TP3 operates at T-7 (decades to centuries). TP4 situates aging within the full temporal hierarchy and shows how T-7 processes are perceived through T-1 mechanisms (fractal fluency of aged surfaces).
L2 operates at T-5 (circadian rhythms). TP4 shows how circadian architecture connects to the full hierarchy.
L5 operates at T-4 (dynamic light changes over hours). TP4 shows how light change rate interacts with occupancy duration.
SC3 operates at T-3 (promenade as composed sequence). TP4 shows that the promenade IS the T-3 level temporal structure of architectural experience.
